issues.legal_issue: A purchaser’s continuous readiness and willingness to perform a sale agreement is assessed from the pleadings, evidence, conduct, and surrounding circumstances, including whether the purchaser had the capacity to pay and whether the seller prevented performance.
material_facts: The purchaser pleaded that it had always been and remained ready and willing to perform the agreement.
The purchaser produced evidence that it prepared a demand draft for a payment due under the agreement and offered that payment to the seller, who refused it.
The seller denied the agreement and did not permit the purchaser to take possession or proceed with the contemplated development, and the courts found that this prevented further performance.
The trial court found that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform, and the seller did not appeal or cross-object against that finding.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform was supported by the evidence and was properly upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 requires a plaintiff seeking specific performance to plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform essential contractual terms, except terms whose performance was prevented or waived by the defendant. Readiness and willingness are not assessed by a straitjacket formula but by considering the party’s conduct and the surrounding circumstances; the purchaser’s capacity, including financial capacity to pay, is relevant. The Court relied on R.C. Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal, (1970) 3 SCC 140; D’Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu, (2004) 6 SCC 649; N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, (1995) 5 SCC 115; and J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao, (2011) 1 SCC 429.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and purchaser_pleaded_continuous_readiness and purchaser_proved_tender_of_due_payment and seller_refused_tender and seller_prevented_subsequent_performance

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The proceeding sought enforcement of an agreement to sell by specific performance.
predicates.purchaser_pleaded_continuous_readiness: The purchaser pleaded that it had always been and remained ready and willing to perform its contractual obligations.
predicates.purchaser_proved_tender_of_due_payment: The purchaser produced evidence that it prepared and offered a payment due under the agreement.
predicates.seller_refused_tender: The seller refused to accept the offered payment.
predicates.seller_prevented_subsequent_performance: The seller’s conduct prevented the purchaser from proceeding with later contractual performance.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeking specific performance pleads continuous readiness, proves a tender that the seller refuses, and is prevented by the seller from proceeding further, the purchaser’s readiness and willingness are established.

issues.legal_issue: An increase in the value of contracted land, without more, does not justify refusing specific performance where no hardship to the seller is pleaded or proved.
material_facts: The trial court refused specific performance because the value of the land had increased.
The seller did not plead hardship or produce evidence that specific performance would be inequitable.
The agreement’s execution and the purchaser’s readiness and willingness to perform had been found proved.
issues.conclusion: The increase in land value alone did not justify denying specific performance, and the appellate court was right to reject that ground for refusing relief.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary, with discretion guided by judicial principles. Under Section 20(2)(c), hardship may justify refusing relief in appropriate circumstances, but mere inadequacy of consideration, an onerous bargain, or an improvident contract does not by itself establish unfair advantage or unforeseeable hardship. The Court relied on K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd., (1999) 5 SCC 77, and also referred to Sargunam (Dead) by LRs. v. Chidambaram, (2005) 1 SCC 162, and Gobind Ram v. Gian Chand, (2000) 7 SCC 548.

rule.if: specific_performance_claim and agreement_execution_proved and purchaser_readiness_and_willingness_established and land_value_increased and seller_hardship_not_proved

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The proceeding sought enforcement of an agreement to sell by specific performance.
predicates.agreement_execution_proved: The evidence established that the agreement to sell had been executed.
predicates.purchaser_readiness_and_willingness_esta: The evidence established the purchaser’s readiness and willingness to perform the agreement.
predicates.land_value_increased: The value of the land increased after the agreement was made.
predicates.seller_hardship_not_proved: The seller neither established hardship nor produced evidence that ordering performance would be inequitable.

issues.definition: If an executed agreement and the purchaser’s readiness to perform are established, an increase in land value without proved seller hardship does not prevent specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: Discretionary appellate review does not warrant disturbing concurrent factual findings on execution and readiness where the findings were not challenged in the lower appellate proceedings and the contrary allegation is unsupported by evidence.
material_facts: The trial court found that the agreement had been executed and that the purchaser was ready and willing to perform.
The seller did not appeal or cross-object against those findings.
The seller’s principal factual defence was that the agreement was fabricated, but the courts found that defence unsupported by evidence.
The Supreme Court considered the matter in appeals invoking its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: There was no valid ground to exercise Article 136 jurisdiction to interfere with the concurrent findings or the decree for specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers discretionary appellate jurisdiction. On the facts here, the Court found no justification to exercise that jurisdiction against concurrent findings supported by the record, particularly where the relevant findings had not been challenged in the lower appellate proceedings and the allegation of fabrication was unproved.

predicates.appeal_under_discretionary_appellate_jur: A party sought discretionary appellate review of a decree enforcing a sale agreement.
predicates.concurrent_findings_on_execution_and_rea: The courts below made concurrent findings that the agreement was executed and the purchaser was ready and willing to perform.
predicates.findings_not_challenged_below: The party seeking review did not challenge those findings by appeal or cross-objection in the lower appellate proceedings.
predicates.fabrication_allegation_unsupported: The party alleged that the agreement was fabricated but produced no evidence substantiating that allegation.

issues.definition: When discretionary appellate review concerns concurrent findings that were not challenged below and the opposing fabrication allegation lacks evidentiary support, appellate interference is declined.
